question: After deciding an agent use case has acceptable benefits and risks, what accountability arrangements should the deployer still establish?
draft:
After accepting the residual risk of an agentic deployment, the deployer should still establish accountability arrangements covering (a) clear allocation of responsibilities within and outside the organisation, and (b) measures enabling meaningful human oversight.

**Residual risk acceptance is not the end point**
Residual risk is the risk remaining after mitigation measures have been applied, and there will always be a level of risk remaining even after identifying appropriate agentic use cases and defining limits on agents; organisations should evaluate and determine whether the residual risk is tolerable and can be accepted [1].

**Clear allocation of responsibilities**
Organisations should consider the allocation of responsibility both within their organisation and vis-à-vis other organisations along the value chain [2]. Within the organisation, organisations should allocate responsibilities for different teams across the agent lifecycle [2]. In the PwC Singapore report-drafting illustration, this allocation is described as: the use case owner remains accountable for responsible use of the application and for ensuring appropriate human oversight is in place [2]; the Technology Risk Management Team supports assessment of technology, risk, security and compliance considerations, including any regulatory requirements, and advises on controls relating to tools and models, access rights, and connected knowledge bases or data sources [2]; and AI Factory designs, develops and maintains the application, including prompt design, model selection, tool configuration, integration with approved knowledge bases and appropriate guardrails, and monitors for model changes and manages updates through standard change management processes rather than leaving it to end users [2].

**External parties**
Where organisations work with external parties when deploying agents (e.g. model developers, agentic AI providers, or hosts of external MCP servers or tools), they should similarly ensure measures are in place to fulfil their own accountability [3]. Agent-specific considerations include clarifying the distribution of obligations in terms and conditions or contracts — in particular provisions on security arrangements, performance guarantees, or data protection — and, where there are gaps, reassessing whether the agentic deployment meets the organisation's risk tolerance [3]. To address third-party opacity, organisations should take steps to maintain sufficient security and control, such as requiring transparency and accountability from external parties (e.g. disclosures on agent capabilities and data handling practices) and requesting and evaluating technical security and control features (e.g. scoped API keys, per-agent identity tokens, and observability such as logging of tool calls and access history); where such features are lacking, organisations should consider alternative or in-house solutions, or scoping down the agentic use case, such as restricting access to sensitive data [3].

**Meaningful human oversight**
The organisations that deploy agents and the humans who oversee them remain accountable for the agents' actions [6]. To address challenges to human accountability — including dynamically emergent agent actions, diffused accountability across multiple stakeholders, and automation bias — organisations should consider clear allocation of responsibilities within and outside the organisation, establishing chains of accountability across the agent value chain and lifecycle while emphasising adaptive governance, and measures to enable meaningful human oversight of agents, such as requiring human approval at significant checkpoints, auditing the effectiveness of human approvals, and complementing these measures with automated monitoring [6].

**Evidence gaps**
The provided excerpts do not establish a specific sequencing requirement that these accountability arrangements be established only after a benefits-and-risks determination, nor do they set deadlines or approval gates for doing so. The excerpts also do not establish whether residual-risk acceptance must be documented or approved by a named body.

Evaluating the residual risks

Residual risk is the risk that remains after mitigation measures have been applied. It is important to note that there will always be a level of risk remaining, even after efforts are taken to identify appropriate agentic use cases and define limits on any agents, especially given how quickly agentic AI is evolving. Ultimately, organisations should evaluate and determine if the residual risk for their agentic deployment is of a tolerable level and can be accepted.

Outside the organisation

Organisations may also need to work with external parties when deploying agents e.g. model developers, agentic AI providers, or hosts of external MCP servers or tools.

In these cases, organisations should similarly ensure that there are measures in place to fulfil its own accountability. Some agent-specific considerations are:

• Clarify distribution of obligations in any terms and conditions or contracts between the organisation and the external party. In particular, organisations should consider provisions on security arrangements, performance guarantees, or data protection. Where there are gaps, the organisation should reassess if the agentic deployment meets its risk tolerance.

• Address third-party opacity: Agents provided by external parties can be difficult to observe and control, making it challenging to understand what information they are grounded on, what they infer from conversations, or how data is stored and used . Organisations should take steps to maintain sufficient security and control, such as: o Require transparency and accountability from external parties e.g. through disclosures on agent capabilities and data handling practices o Request and evaluate technical security and control features e.g. strong authentication measures such as scoped API keys, per -agent identity tokens, and observability such as the logging of tool calls and access history. 2.1.1 Determine suitable use cases for agent deployment

When considering if an agentic use case is suitable for development or deployment , first identify and assess the risk against the benefits. Not all use cases are suitable for agents, and some may be better served by deterministic workflows.

child_citations.title: Policy for the Responsible Use of AI in Government
child_citations.quote:
Agencies should also monitor changes that are not initiated by the agency. For example, vendor changes and changes in the regulatory environment. Agencies could also ask vendors to provide information on updates through contractual mechanisms.

Medium-risk AI use cases If an agency determines their in-scope AI use case has an inherent medium-risk rating when completing an AI use case impact assessment, they should consider if the use case would benefit from being governed through a designated board or a senior executive. Agencies should choose an approach appropriate for the size and scope of the agency if they apply additional governance.

High-risk AI use cases If an agency determines their in-scope AI use case has an inherent high-risk rating when completing an AI use case impact assessment, they must: • report the use case to the agency accountable official with the reasons for the inherent high-risk rating, proposed mitigations and residual risks • govern the use case through a designated board or a senior executive, whichever is appropriate for the size and scope of the agency. Once an agency has decided to deploy the use case, they must: • report the use case to the DTA through the accountable official, see the Standard for accountability • establish a system to regularly review the use case every 12 months at a minimum. The review must report to the relevant governing board or senior executive on whether the use case is operating as intended and that risks are being effectively managed. The review must also consider the AI use case impact assessment and revisions to it, if required.

child_citations.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
child_citations.quote:
2.2 Make humans meaningfully accountable

The organisations that deploy agents and the humans who oversee them remain accountable for the agents’ actions. But it can be challenging to fulfil this accountability when agent actions emerge dynamically and adaptively from interactions instead of fixed logic. Multiple stakeholders may also b e involved in different parts of the agent lifecycle, diffusing accountability. Finally, automation bias, or the tendency to over -trust an automated system, especially when it has performed reliably in the past, becomes a bigger concern as humans supervise increasingly capable agents.

To address these challenges to human accountability, organisations should consider:

• Clear allocation of responsibilities within and outside the organisation , by establishing chains of accountability across the agent value chain and lifecycle, while emphasising adaptive governance, so that the organisation is set up to quickly understand new developments and update their approach as the technology evolves. • Measures to enable meaningful human oversight of agents, such as requiring human approval at significant checkpoints, auditing the effectiveness of human approvals, and complementing these measures with automated monitoring.
